channel.title: Updated · Tech
channel.description: Chips, software, security, devices and space (beyond AI)

item.title: Attackers publish two credential-stealing versions of Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI
item.description: Two malicious releases of Microsoft's agent-framework Python package, downloaded about 200,000 times a month, stole cloud and developer credentials; developers who installed versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 should rebuild and rotate secrets. (BleepingComputer, The Register)

item.title: Intel signs its first outside customer for its 18A chip-making process, and Microsoft adopts its EMIB packaging
item.description: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan says an unnamed company has signed on to make chips with Intel's 18A-P process, and that 18A yields have reached 70%, a step for Intel's effort to compete with TSMC. (Crypto Briefing, TrendForce)

item.title: Microsoft previews Windows Server 2028, which ships hardened by default with post-quantum key exchange
item.description: Windows Server 2028's public preview turns on hundreds of security settings from first boot, including Kerberos over NTLM and hybrid post-quantum TLS, and Microsoft warns that some older software may break. (BleepingComputer, Ars Technica)

item.title: A deployed four-city entanglement-based QKD network with real-time key delivery, benchmarked against finite-key security bounds
item.description: A Slovak quantum key distribution network links four cities over ordinary telecom fiber, runs all links at once and delivers finished keys to applications in real time, with honest post-processed key rates. (Gilberto Borges, Saeid Salari, Ekta Panwar et al. · Institute of Physics, Slovak Academy of Sciences)

item.title: Oracle patches Java4Shell, a Java runtime flaw that lets attackers take over widely used server software
item.description: Oracle fixed a memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder that researchers used to run code on Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak without logging in, and CISA urged immediate patching. (BleepingComputer, The Register, The Record)

item.title: Apple says an internal update, not a cyberattack, knocked out iCloud sign-in, the App Store and other services
item.description: Apple's iCloud sign-in, App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Mail and school tools failed for hours on Tuesday; Apple blamed an internal update and its status page showed everything restored by 6 PM ET. (TechCrunch, BleepingComputer)

item.title: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer is taken offline after an intruder steals user details and login keys
item.description: RIKEN shut down Fugaku on November 14 after an intruder got into internal servers between November 10 and 13 and took details of 4,222 users plus stored login keys. (BleepingComputer, News On Japan, SDxCentral, RIKEN Center for Computational Science)

item.title: California bars Waymo's driverless cars from freeways, and the company halts freeway rides in every market
item.description: California's DMV called Waymo's driverless freeway driving an imminent hazard after robotaxis entered an active construction closure, and Waymo stopped freeway rides across all 15 of its US markets. (TechCrunch, WIRED)

item.title: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence
item.description: Public vulnerability records can show how long a flaw was exploited before a fix existed for only a small share of exploited vulnerabilities, because publishers rarely release patch and vendor dates. (Cédric Bonhomme, Alexandre Dulaunoy · Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg (CIRCL))

item.title: Attackers plant malware on CNN, BBC, Zoom and Salesforce pages through the web-testing service Optimizely
item.description: Attackers abused a flaw in Optimizely's signup flow to add malicious code to scripts that 178 organizations load on their websites, exposing visitors to theft of card details and cryptocurrency. (BleepingComputer, Optimizely)

item.title: The US bars China from renting advanced chips in data centers in five countries and requires licenses for sales there
item.description: A new US Commerce Department rule restricts remote access to advanced chips housed in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, and makes large sales to those countries subject to licenses. (Ars Technica, The Register)

item.title: Italy's privacy regulator fines Meta €805 million because Facebook's Android app read users' photo galleries without specific consent
item.description: Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million ($886 million) over a Facebook feature that scanned Android users' photos and videos to suggest posts, affecting about 20 million people. (The Record, Sky TG24, Garante per la protezione dei dati personali)

item.title: A software bug at JPMorganChase slows payments across US banks, with thousands of customers reporting problems
item.description: JPMorganChase blamed a software bug in its own on-premise systems for slow transactions on Monday that spread to customers of other banks and to Zelle transfers; it says there is no sign of a cyberattack. (WIRED, Engadget)

item.title: An 11-year-old Linux kernel flaw called NoisyTCP lets remote attackers crash servers, and a patch is available
item.description: A flaw in the Linux kernel's TCP code, present for 11 years, lets unauthenticated attackers crash servers over the network; it cannot be used to run code, and a fix is out. (BleepingComputer, Red Hat)

item.title: ULA's Vulcan rocket fails for the first time, destroying 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites
item.description: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after liftoff on Sunday, losing 40 Amazon Leo satellites in the company's first total mission failure since it was formed in 2006. (Ars Technica, The Register, Engadget)

item.title: SpaceX catches a Starship upper stage with its launch tower after nearly a day in orbit
item.description: SpaceX's Starship upper stage returned from orbit on Saturday and was caught by the arms of the launch tower it had left 22 and a half hours earlier, on the first attempt. (Ars Technica, The Register)

item.title: Attackers break into unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell and wipe servers at some Israeli organizations
item.description: Check Point says an attacker used the PHP2Shell flaws and a new privilege-escalation bug to take over unpatched Security Gateways, then wiped VMware ESXi servers at some Israeli organizations. (Check Point Research, BleepingComputer)

item.title: A failure in aging air traffic telecom equipment grounds every US departure for more than four hours
item.description: The FAA halted all US departures on Friday after legacy telecom switches and routers in the air traffic network started passing inconsistent data; officials linked the failure to patches made during an upgrade. (The Verge, WIRED, Ars Technica, Engadget)

item.title: Trezor confirms spy implants in three Safe 5 hardware wallets sold by a Southeast Asian reseller
item.description: Trezor found extra circuit boards in three Safe 5 wallets bought from reseller CryptoBilis that capture recovery phrases from the screen and send them out over a cellular network; new firmware blocks them. (BleepingComputer, Trezor)

item.title: Starship reaches orbit and deploys 26 Starlink satellites, but its booster diverts into the Gulf instead of a tower catch
item.description: SpaceX's 15th Starship flight put 26 Starlink V3 satellites into orbit, but the Super Heavy booster was diverted into the Gulf and exploded; a first attempt to catch the upper stage could come Saturday. (Ars Technica, Next Spaceflight)

item.title: Lessons Not Learned: Why Cross-Chain Bridges Keep Losing Billions the Same Way
item.description: Most cross-chain bridge losses since 2023 came from how bridges were set up, not from code bugs; a rubric scored from on-chain data, plus rate limits and emergency stops, would have cut modeled losses 105-fold. (Mohsen Ahmadvand, Piotr Dobaczewski, Camille Bouzerand · Monad Foundation)

item.title: A Microsoft 365 outage tied to Exchange Online knocks out email, Teams and Copilot for more than 12 hours
item.description: Microsoft 365 services that depend on Exchange Online failed worldwide from Thursday afternoon, and Microsoft's fixes had not brought sustained recovery more than 12 hours later. (BleepingComputer, The Register)

item.title: Apache patches a critical HTTP/2 flaw in its web server that could let attackers run code remotely
item.description: Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 fixes a critical race condition in its HTTP/2 module that could let an unauthenticated attacker run code on servers that have HTTP/2 switched on. (Apache HTTP Server Project, BleepingComputer)

item.title: Police in nine countries seize 235 servers behind the Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC malware
item.description: An Operation Endgame action coordinated by Europol took down 235 servers and 257 domains used by three malware families and found about 6.4 million stolen credentials. (BleepingComputer, The Record)

item.title: Google opens pre-orders for its first Gemini smart glasses, made with Warby Parker, Gentle Monster and Samsung
item.description: Google's camera-equipped "intelligent eyewear," starting at $395, is up for pre-order ahead of a December 10 launch, with privacy limits such as a tamper-checked recording light. (Google, Ars Technica)

item.title: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays
item.description: A design for neutral-atom quantum computers that picks which qubits to operate on by moving helper atoms, letting simple global laser and microwave pulses run error-corrected computation in simulation. (Zhihao Zhang, Shuaifan Cao, Xinyang Yu et al. · Fudan University)

item.title: Attackers push rogue remote-access clients to hundreds of PCs through managed service providers' ScreenConnect panels
item.description: Attackers used cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to install rogue remote-access software on at least 288 computers at 48 organizations; ConnectWise disabled five third-party extensions across about 400 partner environments. (BleepingComputer, Huntress)

item.title: Maersk confirms data theft from a legacy logistics system as a ransomware gang demands $5 million
item.description: Maersk says attackers stole data from an isolated system inherited through an acquisition; the WhiteArmor gang claims about 100GB and wants $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days. (BleepingComputer, The Register)

item.title: The EU proposes a Digital Fairness Act to ban dark patterns, rein in addictive design and limit loot boxes for minors
item.description: The European Commission's draft Digital Fairness Act would ban manipulative "dark patterns," let users switch off addictive features, curb pay-to-win games for minors and allow fines of up to 6% of global turnover. (The Verge, Engadget)

item.title: IBM's quantum roadmap swaps nine linked chips for two larger ones, targeting about 1,040 qubits in 2027
item.description: At its developer conference, IBM said its current Nighthawk r2 chip runs circuits of over 7,500 operations, and planned a 520-qubit Nighthawk r3 for 2027, with two chips linked into a roughly 1,040-qubit system. (IBM Quantum, Ars Technica)

item.title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
item.description: PRISM, a transformer-based decoder for photonic quantum computers, matches slower integer-programming decoders on accuracy and runs on an AMD FPGA with 6.59-microsecond latency. (Daniel Barter, Jacob C. Bridgeman, Chris Dawson et al.)

item.title: France formally blames Iran's Revolutionary Guards for the cyberattacks that heated supermarket freezers
item.description: France says an Iranian Revolutionary Guards cyber unit sabotaged refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores, causing at least 15 fires, and plans to push for EU sanctions. (The Register, TechCrunch)

item.title: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday fixes over 1,000 flaws, including an Outlook bug already used to steal logins
item.description: Microsoft's monthly updates fix between 1,093 and 1,235 vulnerabilities depending on how they are counted, including an exploited Outlook spoofing flaw, alongside patches from Apple, Google, Mozilla and Adobe. (BleepingComputer, Krebs on Security)

item.title: N-able takes its N-central remote-management cloud offline after a researcher publishes 30-plus unpatched flaws
item.description: After a researcher released working exploits for more than 30 alleged flaws without warning, N-able shut down hosted N-central worldwide and told on-premises customers to switch their servers off. (BleepingComputer, TechCrunch)

item.title: Mitsui Chemicals agrees to buy photoresist maker JSR for $11.6 billion
item.description: Mitsui Chemicals will pay 1.84 trillion yen for JSR, a leading maker of the light-sensitive coatings used to print chip circuits, in the largest deal ever in Japan's chemicals sector. (Reuters via The Star, WebProNews)

item.title: SFU-Sim: Bit-Exact Reverse Engineering of NVIDIA MUFU and Validation of PTX Paths
item.description: SFU-Sim reverse-engineers how Nvidia GPUs compute sine, cosine and other special functions, and its model matches real hardware bit for bit on every input across three GPU generations. (Haozhi Xie, Tao Su · Sun Yat-sen University)

item.title: Attackers are exploiting the "SSHole" OpenSSH flaw on Alpine-style Linux servers days after the fix
item.description: Several security firms report real attacks on the OpenSSH and musl flaw CVE-2026-123158, which can give logins to passwordless accounts; OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes it. (Ars Technica, BleepingComputer)

item.title: Vanderbilt University tells campus to shut down devices as the new BYOD ransomware gang claims an attack
item.description: Vanderbilt confirmed an active cyber incident and asked everyone to power off devices; a ransomware group called BYOD claims it stole data on over a million people. (The Record, BleepingComputer)

item.title: Congress summons Nvidia's CEO over a reported Chinese spy operation, and Nvidia's board opens an investigation
item.description: House committee chairs asked Jensen Huang to brief them on November 18 about reported Chinese spying aimed at him; on Sunday Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation. (Ars Technica, TechCrunch, The Verge)

item.title: SonicWall patches a firewall VPN flaw that can sidestep SAML multi-factor login and is already exploited
item.description: SonicWall fixed seven SonicOS flaws, including CVE-2026-19868, which can bypass SAML-enforced MFA on SSL-VPN logins and was added to CISA's catalog of exploited bugs. (SonicWall advisory (as quoted by SecurityWeek), BleepingComputer, Help Net Security)
